lead: A diode or transistor in the op-amp feedback path makes the output proportional to the logarithm of the input voltage. Put an exponential element at the input instead, and the same op-amp gives an antilog. Add two log outputs in a summer and pass the sum through an antilog stage, and the circuit multiplies. Log amplifiers compress a wide range into a few volts, so they serve in decibel readout, RMS measurement, automatic gain control and telephone companding. The circuit is simple; its temperature drift is not.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for the inverting amplifier, Chapter 6.3 for the summing amplifier, the diode equation from Unit 1, and the BJT exponential law from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Build the inverting amplifier of Chapter 6.2, but replace the feedback resistor R_f with a diode. The inverting input is a virtual ground from Chapter 6.1. The input resistor R carries current I = v_in/R into that node. The same current must flow in the diode, because the op-amp input draws no current. A forward-biased diode obeys I = I_S exp(V_D/V_T), so the diode voltage becomes a logarithm of I and therefore of v_in. With the diode connected so that its forward drop is −v_out, the output falls below zero for a positive input.

blocks.where: v_out is the output voltage in volts; v_in is the positive input voltage in volts; V_T is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at 300 K; I_S is the diode reverse saturation current in amperes; R is the input resistor in ohms; ln is the natural logarithm.

blocks.text: v_in must be positive. A negative input reverse-biases the diode, the feedback path opens, and the output saturates near a rail. For a positive input the output is negative, so keep the minus sign. A ×10 increase in v_in raises the diode current by ×10 and changes the diode voltage by V_T ln 10. At 300 K, V_T ≈ 26 mV, so this is 0.026 × 2.303 ≈ 60 mV per decade. The log amp compresses many decades of input into a few volts of output. Both V_T and I_S move with temperature, so the output drifts; that is the main weakness.

Replace the diode with a BJT whose collector is at the virtual ground and whose emitter drives the output, and the same log law appears with the collector current. The BJT holds its exponential relation over more decades than a simple diode, so it is the usual choice in an IC. The equation is still v_out = −V_T ln(v_in/(I_S R)), with I_S now the BJT saturation current. An input of 1 V through 10 kΩ gives 100 µA, a current that a small transistor handles easily.

Uncompensated drift is large. The matched-transistor version uses two identical transistors at the same temperature, one carrying the signal current and one a reference current. Taking the difference of their base-emitter voltages gives a term proportional to ln(I_signal/I_ref); I_S cancels because both transistors have the same I_S. A difference of two logs also removes part of the drift when the same input is measured against a reference. A thermistor or a temperature-sensitive feedback network can correct the remaining V_T drift. At fixed current, a silicon base-emitter voltage falls by about 2 mV for every 1°C rise, so a careless design drifts by millivolts per degree.

An antilog amplifier reverses the blocks. Put the diode or BJT in the input path and a resistor R_f in the feedback path. The input voltage sets the diode current, I = I_S exp(v_in/V_T). That current flows through R_f, so the output is v_out = −I_S R_f exp(v_in/V_T). The output is an exponential of the input. The input range is small, often only a few hundred millivolts, because the exponential rises fast.

To multiply, take the log of each input, add the two logs, and take the antilog. The identity is ln v₁ + ln v₂ = ln(v₁v₂). A summer from Chapter 6.3 performs the addition. The antilog stage turns the sum back into a product. With scaling, the output is v_out = v₁v₂/k, where v₁ and v₂ are positive input voltages in volts, v_out is the output voltage, and k is a scaling voltage in volts set by the antilog reference. For v₁ = 2 V, v₂ = 3 V and k = 10 V, v_out = 0.6 V. Change the summer to subtraction and the same chain divides: ln v₁ − ln v₂ = ln(v₁/v₂). Feed one input to both logs and it squares.

These blocks are used for decibel readout, RMS-to-DC conversion, companding in telephony, automatic gain control and power measurement. Most integrated multipliers use a Gilbert cell, a variable-transconductance circuit; only a few syllabi analyze its internals. Treat the log–antilog chain as the explanation of the function, not as the only hardware.

figure.caption: Each input is log-amplified, the two logs are added in the summing amplifier, and the antilog stage returns the product divided by k. The numbers are those of the worked example: 2 V and 3 V give 0.6 V with k = 10 V.

spec.title: Log–antilog multiplier
spec.aria: A multiplier built from logarithms: each input is log-amplified, the two logs are added, and an antilog stage turns the sum back into the product.

examples.question: A diode log amplifier has R = 10 kΩ, I_S = 10⁻¹⁴ A and V_T = 26 mV. Find v_out for v_in = 1 V, then for v_in = 0.1 V, and the change per decade. Then find the output of a log–antilog multiplier with v₁ = 2 V, v₂ = 3 V and scaling voltage k = 10 V.
steps: Input current at 1 V: I₁ = v_in/R = 1 V / 10,000 Ω = 0.0001 A = 100 µA.
Current ratio: I₁/I_S = 100 × 10⁻⁶ A / 10⁻¹⁴ A = 1.0 × 10¹⁰. Natural log: ln(1.0 × 10¹⁰) = 23.0259.
Input current at 0.1 V: I₂ = 0.1 V / 10,000 Ω = 0.00001 A = 10 µA. Ratio I₂/I_S = 1.0 × 10⁹ and ln(1.0 × 10⁹) = 20.7233.
Change from 1 V to 0.1 V: v_out2 − v_out1 = −0.5388 V − (−0.5987 V) = 0.0599 V. The magnitude is 59.9 mV per decade; for a ×10 increase in input, the signed change is −0.0599 V.
Multiplier output: v_out = v₁v₂/k = (2 V × 3 V) / 10 V = 0.6 V.
examples.answer: v_out ≈ −0.5987 V at 1 V, ≈ −0.5388 V at 0.1 V, a magnitude of ≈59.9 mV (0.0599 V) per decade; the multiplier output is 0.6 V.
examples.check:
import math
R = 10e3
IS = 1e-14
VT = 0.026
v1_in = 1.0
v2_in = 0.1
I1 = v1_in / R
I2 = v2_in / R
vout1 = -VT * math.log(I1 / IS)
vout2 = -VT * math.log(I2 / IS)
decade = vout2 - vout1
mult = (2.0 * 3.0) / 10.0
print(round(vout1, 4))
print(round(vout2, 4))
print(round(decade, 4))
print(round(mult, 4))

traps: Dropping the minus sign: a positive v_in gives a negative v_out in the inverting log amplifier.
Forgetting temperature: V_T and I_S both move, so an uncompensated log amp drifts by millivolts per degree.
Applying a negative or zero input: the diode cuts off, the feedback path opens, and the log law fails.
Swapping the positions: a log amp has the diode in the feedback path; an antilog amp has the diode in the input path.
Using v_out = v₁v₂ without scaling: the multiplier output is v₁v₂/k and must stay inside the op-amp rails.

quiz.q: Which element is in the feedback path of a diode log amplifier?
quiz.a: A diode. The input resistor R sets I = v_in/R, and the diode converts that current to a logarithmic voltage.

quiz.q: Why is the log-amp slope about 60 mV per decade at 300 K?
quiz.a: A ×10 current change changes the diode voltage by V_T ln 10 = 0.026 V × 2.303 ≈ 0.060 V, that is 60 mV.

quiz.q: A diode log amplifier has R = 10 kΩ, I_S = 10⁻¹⁴ A and V_T = 26 mV. Find v_out for v_in = 0.5 V.
What does a matched transistor pair cancel in a log amplifier, and what does it not cancel?
quiz.a: It cancels I_S by taking the difference of two base-emitter voltages at the same temperature. It does not cancel the V_T temperature drift, which needs additional compensation.

quiz.q: Write the output of an antilog amplifier with a diode in the input path and R_f in feedback.
quiz.a: v_out = −I_S R_f exp(v_in/V_T), where I_S is the diode saturation current, R_f is the feedback resistor, and V_T is the thermal voltage.

quiz.q: A log–antilog multiplier has v₁ = 1.5 V, v₂ = 4 V and k = 10 V. Find v_out.
quiz.a: v_out = v₁v₂/k = (1.5 V × 4 V) / 10 V = 6 V² / 10 V = 0.6 V.

quiz.q: How does a log–antilog chain divide one voltage by another?
quiz.a: Subtract the logs: ln v₁ − ln v₂ = ln(v₁/v₂). The antilog stage turns the difference back into v₁/v₂, scaled by the reference voltage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Integrated logarithmic detectors are used in RF power meters and optical receivers because they turn a wide dynamic range into a linear voltage. RMS-to-DC converter ICs use similar log and antilog blocks to compute a true RMS value without a thermal sensor. Audio companding and automatic gain control still use exponential control of gain. Search for Gilbert cell multiplier, logarithmic detector and RMS-to-DC converter to see the industrial versions.
